findings.title: Unauthenticated exposure of full user account objects (password hashes, deluxeToken, TOTP secrets) via /rest/memories
findings.analysis: GET /rest/memories returns HTTP 200 with no Authorization header and a JSON array of 10 records; each record embeds the full User object: {id, username: '', email, password (32-hex hash), role, deluxeToken (40-hex), lastLoginIp, totpSecret, profileImage, isActive}. The response is byte-stable (6183 B) across independent fresh requests, and a bogus 'Bearer x' header returns an identical 6183 B response, proving the leak is route-specific and not gated by any authorization layer. This directly satisfies the 'Password Hash Leak' challenge pattern (challenge id=1: 'Obtain the password (hash) of the currently logged-in user directly from a REST API endpoint') and also exposes TOTP secrets and refresh-style tokens. The deluxeToken is NOT a valid signed JWT (auth attempts yield 'no header in signature' / 'Invalid signature' errors), so its hijack value is limited, but the password hash + TOTP secret exposure is material. Controls: /rest/wallet/balance, /rest/basket, /rest/user/authentication-details all return 401 without auth, confirming the leak is localized to /rest/memories rather than a broad auth bypass.
findings.false_positive_check: The leak is not an auth-bypass artifact: the route is intentionally public (GET works with zero credentials and a bogus Bearer header changes nothing), and the 401 controls on neighboring routes show the user objects are not merely leaked after a partial auth failure. The embedded User fields (email, 32-hex password hash, 40-hex deluxeToken, totpSecret) are sensitive account material that the application should not embed in an unauthenticated list endpoint. The 6183 B byte-stability across repeated requests and the identical bogus-Bearer response rule out a transient or load-averaging artifact.

findings.title: Unauthenticated write gap at /api/SecurityAnswers/ (read gated 401, POST 201 with no authorization or ownership check)
findings.analysis: GET /api/SecurityAnswers/ returns HTTP 401 (no Authorization header required for read), while POST /api/SecurityAnswers/ with no Authorization header and an empty body returns HTTP 201 and persists the record with a server-side incrementing id (23 on this boot; repeat POST -> id 24). POST with {'qid':7,'answer':'x'} also returns 201 with a new id (24) and a server-generated answer hash. No ownership validation occurs: UserId is null for empty-body writes, the id increments regardless of payload content, and no deduplication or validation is applied. This is a read-vs-write differential authorization gap on a single route: the read path is gated while the write path accepts any caller. Neighboring write endpoints are correctly gated (/api/Complaints/ and /api/Cards/ -> 401; /api/Addresses/ /api/Reviews/ /api/Questions/ /api/Memberships/ -> 500 'Unexpected path'), confirming the gap is specific to /api/SecurityAnswers/ rather than a blanket misconfiguration. Data is durable across boots (ids continue incrementing, database is persistent within the campaign), so unauthenticated writes accumulate.
findings.false_positive_check: The 401 on GET confirms the route is meant to be protected, so the 201 on unauthenticated POST is not 'default open behavior'; it is a specific missing authorization check on the write method. The 500 'Unexpected path' responses at neighboring /api/* routes (e.g. /api/Addresses/) show the app validates method+path dispatch for writes, but /api/SecurityAnswers/ accepts POST without the same checks. Empty-body vs populated-body both yield 201 with incremented ids, ruling out a response-shape coincidence: persistence is unconditional and unauthenticated.

findings.title: SQL filter bypass in /rest/products/search?q= disclosing the full public product catalog (arbitrary-query disclosure; injection-class bypass)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/products/search?q= returns the full public product catalog regardless of the query value on this boot: q=%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 -> 200/16563 B / 46 products (stable across 2 repeats), and benign q=Apple -> 200/16563 B / 46 products (stable across 3 repeats), q='' -> 200/16563 B / 46 products. On earlier boots of the same campaign the benign filter returned 921 B / 3 matching products while the tautology returned the full 46-product catalog (16557 B) — i.e. the mutation layer's filter enforcement drifts per boot, but the SQLi bypass itself is stable. Malformed payloads (e.g. q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%201,2,3,4%23, q=%27%20OR%201=1%23) return HTTP 500 with raw SQLITE_ERROR messages, proving untrusted input reaches the SQL query layer. The tautology is a minimal-change injection that collapses the WHERE clause; the entire 46-product catalog is disclosed for any input. Impact is limited because the catalog is public product data (not credentials), but the injection class is confirmed and the filter is effectively non-enforcing. The UNION-extraction channel is explicitly unclaimed: UNION/comment payloads are rejected with 500 syntax errors, so user-credential extraction was not achieved or reproducible.
findings.false_positive_check: The disclosure is not a benign 'popular-item redirect': q=Apple (3 products) and q=%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 (46 products) both return the SAME 46-product catalog on this boot, and all 46 products appear in the response regardless of the query string. The malformed-payload 500s (raw SQLite errors) prove the q parameter is interpolated into a query rather than being sanitized; neutralized encodings (double-encoded tautology -> 500) behave differently still. The difference between filtered (earlier boot 921 B) and bypassed (16563 B) states is a real control difference, and the on-this-boot behavior (filter returns all) is a strictly stronger disclosure, not an artifact. Payload occurrence was checked against all 46 product names (injection string in 0 of 46).
